summary: MADAR (مدار, which means "orbit" in Arabic) is a browser game in which students develop a space mission from scratch – design, launch and pilot a spacecraft. In the game, students select one of four problems that exist in the world such as monitoring coral reefs around Bahrain, monitoring fires and floods, detecting water ice on Mars, and monitoring the storms on Jupiter. The next step is selecting a satellite composed of 15 components, setting an orbit and a launching rocket and staying within budget, mass, power, memory and building time constraints. Each decision comes with its price, for example, more components will require more energy, more energy will require heavier solar panels and, accordingly, a larger rocket. A group of up to four players (the roles of Scientist, Comms, Engineer, and Pilot), decide whether to GO or NO GO and then pilot the mission, take pictures and send information to the control center while avoiding the danger of debris and solar flares. In conclusion, students provide reasons why their mission was successful or not and offer a "what if" solution. Finally, a real NASA fact is presented.
details:
What it does and how it works
MADAR is a browser game for 1 to 4 players in which students design and run a whole space mission. A mission has six steps. 1) Choose a real problem (Gulf Reef Watch, Disaster Alert, Mars Water Hunter, or Jupiter Storm Chaser) and promise how many targets you will deliver. 2) Build a satellite from 15 parts, with live mass, power, cost, memory, and build-time numbers and warnings. 3) Choose an orbit altitude, an orbit type (equatorial, polar, or sun-synchronous), and a rocket. The game checks whether the rocket can lift your satellite. 4) A team council of four roles (Scientist, Comms, Engineer, Pilot) votes GO or NO GO. 5) Fly the mission live: take pictures of targets, send data when a ground station is in range, switch to power save, and dodge debris and solar flares. 6) A report gives a score, stars, a “why it worked or failed” list, a “what if” suggestion from an autopilot replay, and a real NASA fact.

Benefits and impact
Students usually meet orbits, power, mass, and communications in separate lessons. MADAR puts them in one decision chain, so players feel that a better camera needs more power, which needs bigger solar panels, which adds mass and cost. Mission numbers are based on real missions such as Landsat, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Juno. Teams must talk and agree, which also practices the teamwork real missions need.

Tools used
HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript (ES modules) with the HTML5 Canvas for the flight screen. There are no frameworks, no install, and no hardware. We used VS Code, GitHub, and GitHub Pages for hosting. All balance numbers live in one data file, so the game is easy to adjust.

Creativity
MADAR has an Arabian desert night design with arch-shaped panels, a camel caravan, and a crescent moon, and it is built around Bahrain’s own reefs. After the countdown, a dark page shows an Arabic poem line by line before the flight begins. This gives each launch a moment of calm and ties the mission to Arab poetry and travel by the stars. Buttons make a click sound. Players can share a design code or a challenge code so other teams can fly the same mission and compare results. Each mission teaches a different lesson: shadow and batteries on Earth, long-distance data on Mars, and radiation and weak sunlight at Jupiter.

What we considered
We balanced realism against clarity for students, kept every rule explainable on the results screen, and made it accessible with no accounts or downloads. We chose the missions to cover the main trade-offs: orbit type, power, communications, protection, budget, and time.
